Chapter 8: Navigating Conflict and Repairing Relationships.
Even when you’re building healthier patterns and growing in self-awareness, let’s be honest—conflict’s just a part of life. We all bump into it. The real difference isn’t whether conflict happens, but how you handle it when it does. Imagine approaching conflict from your Adult state. Suddenly, it’s not something to fear—it’s actually a chance to grow, to understand each other better, and to make your relationship even stronger.
So, where do you start? Well, first, it helps to spot those early warning signs: maybe you notice tension rising, you feel yourself getting defensive, or maybe you just want to shut down and walk away. Those are usually clues that some old patterns, those familiar scripts or ego states, are kicking in.
Here’s what really helps in these moments:
Pause for a second and ask yourself, “Which part of me is showing up right now? Am I reacting like a Parent, an Adult, or a Child?”
If you notice you’re stuck in a less helpful state, try to shift back into your Adult mode. And it’s totally okay to take a breather if you need it—sometimes stepping away helps you respond, instead of react.
Once you’re ready, name the issue clearly and respectfully. You might say, “I feel upset about what happened earlier. Can we talk about it?” It’s simple, but it invites real conversation, not just another round of blame or avoidance.
Now, when it comes to repairing relationships after there’s been a blow-up or hurt feelings, it takes courage. You’ve got to be willing to get a little vulnerable and really listen. That means:
Owning your part—maybe saying, “Hey, I realize I was harsh. I’m sorry.”
Letting the other person share their side, without jumping in or defending yourself.
And then, working together to find a solution that works for both of you.
Of course, sometimes, those old hurts or deep-rooted patterns make things tougher. If that’s the case, it can be really helpful to bring in some outside support, or to set up a few ground rules before diving into those tough conversations.
But here’s something really important to remember: the goal isn’t to avoid conflict altogether. Instead, you’re learning to use conflict as a way to build more trust and understanding. Every time you work through a disagreement with honesty and care, your relationship actually gets stronger, more resilient.
And over time, these skills start to feel natural. Disagreements don’t seem so scary anymore—they’re just chances to practice empathy, assertiveness, and collaboration. That “I’m OK – You’re OK” mindset gets steadier, even when things get tough.
